rationale: B wins because it keeps the strongest story honest: "Chipotle says it won't raise prices this year, even as its food costs climb" is clean, pitchable, and explicitly warns that the facts do not prove automation funds the price hold. A has good bones, but its lead angle, "Chipotle bets a robot can hold the line on menu prices," smuggles in the causal claim a reporter will immediately attack. That is not polish; that is the difference between a real angle and a booby trap in a better suit.
gaps_in_A: "Chipotle bets a robot can hold the line on menu prices" overconnects two facts. The update says Chipotle is rolling out Autocado and holding prices flat; it does not say the robot enables the price freeze.
"automation as the implied offset" is the dangerous sentence. Implied by whom? Unless Chipotle or unit economics connects those dots, this is inference wearing a press badge.
"The prevailing belief right now is that chains pass food-cost inflation straight to the menu" may be plausible, but it is outside the supplied facts and should be sourced or softened.
The set knows its own problem but does not fix it: "is automation savings the real offset, or is that an inference you can't yet support?" belongs before the headline is written, not after it.
gaps_in_B: "Food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory" is useful color, but it is not in the update. Source it or cut it.
"100 stores is the pilot-to-deployment threshold this beat watches for" sounds authoritative without evidence. Do not invent a beat rule because the sentence wants rhythm.
"Restaurant robots leave the pilot phase" is a little too tidy when the proof section later asks whether 100 stores is "a committed first wave or a larger pilot." Pick one level of certainty.
B could have called out the most likely reporting trap more bluntly: the Digital Makeline is only "testing," so it cannot carry much weight beyond supporting context.
